cards.title: 5W Avatar Framework for Ecommerce Market Research
cards.summary: A five-question framework (Who, What, When, Where, Why) for defining an ecommerce customer avatar before writing marketing copy or building offers.
cards.use_when: Starting a new business, launching a new offer, or entering a new niche and you need a structured avatar before producing marketing assets.
steps: Who: capture three layers — demographics (age, gender, income, occupation), geographics (city, state, province, country), and psychographics (values, attitudes, beliefs, lifestyles).

What: separate 'miracles' (wants, dreams, goals, desired outcomes) from 'miseries' (fears, frustrations, pains, problems). Write these as two distinct lists because they feed different marketing angles.

When: identify life events that shift buying decisions (marriage, divorce, new child, new job, moving) and daily schedules that affect consumption timing (traditional 9-5 vs. stay-at-home parent vs. home entrepreneur).

Where: locate where the avatar is present online and offline — which platforms they read, watch and socialize on. A quick search for 'social media demographics' shows which platforms skew to which groups.
Why: dig into the deeper motivations behind wanting the benefits — why those benefits matter to them personally.
If launching to an existing market, identify your top 20% of customers and look for shared patterns across demographics, geographics and psychographics rather than working from assumptions.
caveats: The framework is a baseline research structure, not a validation method on its own — pair it with the intent-mining methods to confirm real demand.
The source notes it wrote a 'jingle' as a memory aid; the framework itself, not the mnemonic, is the substance.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Avoid Focus Groups and Leading Surveys for Market Research
cards.summary: Traditional market research methods such as focus groups, badly worded surveys, and academic white papers are flagged as expensive, biased or outdated compared with direct intent mining.
cards.use_when: Choosing which research method to invest time and budget in, or deciding whether a proposed focus group or survey is worth running.
steps: Treat focus groups as low priority: the source calls them expensive, hard to get in-depth data from, and prone to moderator bias, where the person running the group injects opinions and sways direction through how questions are framed.

Treat surveys as fragile: rephrasing a question from positive to negative can change results, leading questions skew responses before the respondent thinks, and question order plus the survey's own description can prime answers.
Treat academic white papers and research reports as often too academic or theoretical for real-world use, and potentially outdated the moment they are published, especially in fast-moving industries.
Substitute direct behaviour data: mine what people actually search (Google), what they actually buy (Amazon), and what competitors actually spend on (Meta Ad Library).
If you must use a survey, expect to invest heavily in neutral wording and careful interpretation rather than treating results as clean data.
caveats: These are the presenter's strong opinions about method trade-offs, not a universal rule; focus groups and surveys can still be appropriate where qualitative depth or statistically representative samples are genuinely required.
The critique applies to poorly constructed versions specifically — the source cites leading questions, framing effects and moderator bias as the failure modes.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Google Autocomplete to Map Search Intent
cards.summary: Use Google's autocomplete suggestions to enumerate long-tail search intent around a core niche keyword before sizing volume.
cards.use_when: Early niche or offer research when you need to discover the language and sub-topics your market actually searches for.
steps: Type your main niche keyword into Google without pressing enter and read the autocomplete suggestions that appear after it.

Work through the suggestions that look relevant to your business, then keep typing a promising stem to surface deeper suggestions (e.g. typing a seed phrase yields further suggestions like 'for beginners', a file format, or a tool type).
Record the relevant suggestions as candidate topics or sub-niches; relevance depends on whether your business is product- or service-based, so filter accordingly.
Evaluate each promising term for overall search volume — the source uses Google Ads Keyword Planner for this, but verify the current interface and workflow in Google Ads before relying on it.
The source chose a deliberately obscure example niche to show the method works for almost anything, so do not skip this step just because your niche feels too niche.
caveats: Autocomplete shows what people type, not how many people type it — you need a volume tool to judge size.
Search volume reflects stated intent, not purchase behaviour; pair with purchase intent data before committing.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Size Niche Keywords and Spot Seasonality in Keyword Planner
cards.summary: Use Google Ads Keyword Planner's 'discover new keywords' flow to pull keyword ideas with volume, competition and trend data for a target geography.
cards.use_when: After autocomplete mining, when you need to size demand, compare sub-topics, or check whether a niche has seasonal patterns.
steps: Log into Google Ads, open Keyword Planner, and choose the option to discover new keywords (verify the current label and location in the present Google Ads interface, as menus change).
Enter your seed search term and select the geographic pool you want to research — the source used US and Canada as an example.
Review the returned list of keyword ideas, which the source describes as over a thousand for a single seed term, along with search volume and competition.
Use the data to check overall competition in the niche, spot trends and seasonality, and decide which sub-topics are worth building content or offers around.
Sort and prioritise terms, but keep judgment: volume and competition are inputs, not a mandate to target every high-volume term.
caveats: Volume ranges in Keyword Planner are estimates and should be treated as directional, not exact.
The source found its example niche surprisingly competitive once volume was checked — expect your assumptions about a niche's size to be corrected.
Tool navigation is version-dependent; confirm current steps in Google Ads.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Amazon Autocomplete and Book Titles for Purchase Intent
cards.summary: Amazon surfaces what people actually buy via autocomplete, optimized book titles/subtitles, and listing copy that reflects real market language.
cards.use_when: Validating that a niche has real buyers and harvesting market-tested language, after search-intent research on Google.
steps: Search your main keyword on Amazon and read the autocomplete suggestions; the source notes they often look similar to Google's but reflect shopping behaviour rather than information seeking.

Hit enter and study the book titles and subtitles in the niche — because books take far longer to produce than a blog or social post, authors spend significant effort optimizing titles, subtitles and descriptions to appeal to the exact target demographic.
Treat that book copy as pre-optimized marketing language you can mine for headline and offer phrasing.
Check the products and categories returned to see what formats the market actually pays for.
If your niche has no meaningful book presence, adapt the same logic to the most heavily optimized listings in the category.
caveats: Book title language is optimized for a publishing market, which may not map perfectly onto your product category.
Amazon search results are a snapshot of current listings; check whether the niche's book presence is genuine rather than incidental.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Amazon Review Mining and Review-Count Sales Estimation
cards.summary: Read Amazon reviews to extract what buyers liked and disliked, and use review counts as a rough proxy for sales velocity.
cards.use_when: Estimating demand and gathering voice-of-customer language for a specific product or niche on Amazon.
steps: Open listings in your niche and read the reviews for what buyers specifically liked and did not like about what they bought — this is the primary data source.
Use those likes and dislikes to shape product angles, objection handling and copy themes.
Estimate relative sales volume by comparing the number of reviews a listing has received; the source presents this as a rough guess, since exact units sold are not visible.
Compare review counts across competing listings to rank which products are moving.
Feed the extracted language into your marketing angle alongside the avatar's miracles and miseries.
caveats: Review counts are only a rough proxy for sales — they depend on review rates, listing age and seller practices, so do not treat them as precise sales figures.
The source explicitly frames this as a guess, not a measurement.
Review sentiment can be gamed or skewed by a small number of vocal buyers.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Facebook Ad Library to Identify Profitable Competitor Angles
cards.summary: Use Meta's Ad Library via a competitor's Page Transparency to find which ad angles have run longest, as duration is treated as a proxy for profitability.
cards.use_when: Researching competitor messaging and offer angles in industries with active Meta advertising, after you have defined your avatar.
steps: Go to Facebook, search for your industry or a specific competitor's page, and open that page.
Scroll to the 'Page Transparency' section and click to see all details.
If the page is running ads, click through to the Ad Library so all of their ads appear.
Study each ad, paying special attention to ads that appear repeatedly and to those closest to the bottom of the feed, which indicates they have run the longest.
Treat long-running ads as the most likely to be profitable relative to the others, then adapt the underlying angle rather than copying the creative.
Repeat across as many competitors as possible who advertise on Facebook or Instagram.
caveats: The source states that longer-running generally means more profitable, but adds that this is not always the case — do due diligence before assuming.
Some industries (the source contrasts a niche craft example with health and fitness) have far fewer competitor ads available to study.
Requires ads to be publicly visible in the library; ad library coverage and interface details change and should be verified.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Separate What Customers Say From What They Buy
cards.summary: Stated wants (search behaviour) and actual purchases (retail behaviour) are two different datasets and both are required for useful market research.
cards.use_when: Designing a research plan or deciding how much weight to give survey-style stated preferences versus behavioural evidence.
steps: Capture what people say they want using search engines — the source treats search queries as the best available proxy for stated desire, mined via Google autocomplete and Keyword Planner.
Capture what people actually buy using Amazon — autocomplete, optimized book titles, and review data reflecting completed purchases.
Treat the two as complementary: stated wants shape marketing language and campaign copy; actual purchases confirm real demand.
Apply the principle that talk is cheap — asking whether someone would buy something is different from putting the product in front of them and asking for payment.
When the two datasets disagree, weight behavioural evidence more heavily for offer and product decisions, and stated language for messaging.
caveats: Search intent still over-represents researchers versus buyers; it is an indication, not a guarantee of purchase.
The source's core claim is that stated-vs-actual must be distinguished, not that either dataset is sufficient alone.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Miracles and Miseries Extraction for Marketing Angles
cards.summary: Convert avatar research into two concrete lists — desired outcomes and pains — and turn them into marketing angles.
cards.use_when: Moving from raw avatar research into copy themes, ad angles and offer framing.
steps: List 'miracles': all of the wants, dreams, goals and desires the avatar is hoping to obtain.
List 'miseries': all of the fears, frustrations, pains and problems they are trying to get away from.
Keep the lists explicit and specific rather than summarising them into generic categories, because the specific items become the angles.
Use miracles to write aspirational messaging and offer promises.
Use miseries to write problem-agitation messaging and objection handling.
Cross-check the lists against what you found in purchase intent data so angles are grounded in real buying behaviour, not assumption.
caveats: This is qualitative synthesis; the source does not provide thresholds or weighting for how many items are enough.
Miseries stated in research can be exaggerated or socially shaped — validate against purchase behaviour before building a whole campaign on one.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Research Top 20% of Existing Customers for a New Offer
cards.summary: When launching a new offer to an existing audience, base the avatar on your top 20% of customers rather than on imagined demographics.
cards.use_when: You already have a customer base and are preparing a new offer, upsell or product line for that same market.
steps: Identify your top 20% of customers — the segment the source treats as the highest-value reference group.

Look for shared patterns across three categories: demographics (age, gender, income, occupation), geographics (city, state, province, country), and psychographics (values, attitudes, beliefs, lifestyles).
Cross-reference those patterns with the miracles and miseries lists to understand what this segment is buying and avoiding.
Use the resulting shared profile to shape the new offer's positioning rather than reusing a generic avatar from a previous launch.
If the offer is genuinely new to a new market instead, switch to studying competitors' ads and targeting to infer the audience.
caveats: The 'top 20%' figure is the source's framing without a stated method for ranking customers — define your own ranking metric (revenue, repeat purchase, margin) and document it.
Survivorship bias applies: your existing best customers may not represent the wider addressable market for a new offer.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Social Media Demographics Search for Platform Placement
cards.summary: A quick search for platform demographic data tells you which groups use which social channels, informing where to place content.
cards.use_when: Deciding which platforms to prioritise for content and campaigns based on your avatar's actual presence.
steps: Complete the 'Where' step of the avatar framework first by noting where your audience reads, watches, socialises and engages online and offline.
Run a quick search for a term like 'social media demographics' to find which kinds of people use which platforms.
Match your avatar's demographic and psychographic profile against those platform skews.
Prioritise content production on the platforms where your avatar is actually active, then expand once you have evidence.
Use this as an input to the creative and distribution brief rather than running ads directly from this step.
caveats: Demographic data sources vary in methodology and are usually revised; confirm figures from a current, credible source rather than relying on a single page.
Platform demographics describe averages, not your specific niche — validate against your own audience data where available.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Life Events and Daily Schedules as Buying Triggers
cards.summary: The 'When' lens targets moments in the customer's life and day that change buying behaviour and content consumption.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign timing, seasonal pushes, or content scheduling around your avatar's routines and transitions.
steps: Scan for life events that alter or influence buying decisions — the source lists marriage, divorce, a new child, a new job, and moving to a new city as examples.
Map how each event changes needs and what the avatar is looking for immediately after it.
Examine day-to-day schedules to determine when and where they consume content or make buying decisions.
Contrast schedule types explicitly — the source distinguishes a traditional 9-5 worker from a stay-at-home parent or home entrepreneur, treating them as materially different buying contexts.
Use the timing findings to schedule sends, posts and ad flights to match when the avatar is actually reachable.
caveats: Life-event research identifies correlation with buying windows, not proof that the event caused a purchase.
No specific timing benchmarks are given, so test scheduling assumptions rather than assuming them.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Demographic, Geographic and Psychographic Layering for Ecommerce Avatars
cards.summary: Build the 'Who' layer as three stacked dimensions — demographics, geographics and psychographics — rather than demographics alone.
cards.use_when: Constructing an avatar document that will be handed to copywriters, media buyers or creative teams.
steps: Demographic details: age, gender, income, occupation.
Geographic details: city, state or province, country — relevant for shipping, regional language and channel selection.
Psychographic details: values, attitudes, beliefs and lifestyles.
When basing the avatar on an existing customer base, compare these three categories across your top customers to find shared traits rather than listing every variation.
When the offer is new, infer the three categories from competitors' ads and targeting instead of guessing.
Keep all three layers visible when writing copy — demographics alone produce generic messaging.
caveats: Psychographics are inferred from behaviour and interviews, so they are less reliable than demographic fields.
Geographic segmentation matters less for purely digital delivery but still affects channel and language choices.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Boundary Between Research, Creative, Media and Web Work
cards.summary: Market research and avatar work sits upstream of ad production, media buying and landing-page implementation and should hand off cleanly.
cards.use_when: Scoping who does what when planning a launch so research outputs are not confused with execution deliverables.
steps: Keep in the research phase: baseline qualitative and quantitative frameworks for defining avatars, extracting pain points, and validating demand via search intent, purchase intent and competitor ad libraries.
Hand off copywriting and creative asset production to the creative function rather than doing it during research.
Hand off launching and managing paid media campaigns to the media execution function.
Hand off implementing the messaging on landing pages to the storefront/site function.
Deliver research outputs as inputs — avatar profile, miracles and miseries lists, keyword map, competitor angle list — and let downstream owners apply them.
caveats: These boundaries come from one internal operating model and may need adapting to small teams where one person covers several stages.
The research phase produces direction, not finished copy or media plans.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Judge Whether an Ad's Longevity Signals Profitability
cards.summary: Ad duration is a usable but imperfect proxy for profitability; apply informed judgment and corroborate before treating a long-running ad as proven.
cards.use_when: Screening competitor ads in the Meta Ad Library and deciding which angles to model or test.
steps: Sort attention to ads at the bottom of the competitor's ad library feed, since these have run the longest.
Also note ads that recur repeatedly across your scan — repetition is treated as a second signal.
Interpret duration as an indication that the advertiser keeps paying for it, which suggests it is producing better results than their alternatives.
Corroborate before acting: the source explicitly says running longest is not always the same as most profitable, so do due diligence rather than copying on duration alone.
Combine the surviving angles with your own miracles/miseries research and keyword data to build a test slate.
caveats: Duration can also reflect campaigns left running by neglect, always-on brand ads, or ads with low spend — the underlying assumption is the presenter's, not a measured fact.
Ad Library visibility and sorting behaviour can change; verify the current interface.
Only applies where competitors actually run ads on Meta.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx

cards.title: Why Deeper Motivation Belongs in the Avatar
cards.summary: The 'Why' step converts features and benefits into motivation, telling you which benefits to lead with.
cards.use_when: Writing the value proposition or offer copy after the Who, What, When and Where steps are complete.
steps: For each benefit your offer provides, ask why that benefit matters to the avatar personally.
Check whether the customer would actually benefit from your specific offer, not just from the generic category.
Record the chain from feature to benefit to underlying motivation so copywriters can pick the right lead.
Cross-check the motivation against the miracles list — the stated desire and the underlying driver should align or the discrepancy should be noted.
Use the deeper driver to decide which benefit gets headline placement versus supporting copy.
caveats: Why-level motivations are interpretive and can be wrong; validate with purchase behaviour and customer conversations where possible.
The source offers no method for ranking motivations against each other — prioritise by evidence from your own customers.
cards.source_name: How To Do Market Research (Market Research 101).docx
